# NGC 1275: Reading the Record of Perseus A

*SIMBAD identifies this galaxy as a blazar and a cD system, and records its position, apparent angular size and redshift.*

NGC 1275 has more than one name in the astronomical record: SIMBAD lists it as both NGC 1275 and Perseus A. The database classifies it as a blazar and gives its morphological type as cD. These labels describe different aspects of how the object is categorized. They are useful starting points for understanding its place in astronomy, but they do not, by themselves, tell an observer how bright it will appear in an eyepiece or what details a particular telescope can reveal.

The classifications also illustrate why astronomical catalogues are best read as records, not as complete portraits. SIMBAD identifies the source of its cD designation as a 2020 study, while its blazar classification appears among the object types associated with catalogues and references. The database’s entry gathers those classifications alongside measured and catalogued properties. It does not provide a detailed account of the processes behind the galaxy’s activity, so those should not be inferred from the labels alone. [SIMBAD’s NGC 1275 entry](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=NGC%201275)

The entry gives NGC 1275’s J2000 coordinates as right ascension 3 hours, 19 minutes and 48.16 seconds, and declination +41 degrees, 30 minutes and 42.11 seconds. These coordinates are a precise way to specify a location on the sky. Right ascension is expressed in hours, minutes and seconds; declination gives the position north or south of the celestial equator. The J2000 label identifies the coordinate reference frame used in the catalogue. For someone preparing to locate the object, these numbers can be entered into a planetarium program or used to check a star chart.

SIMBAD also lists an optical angular size of 2.63 by 1.78 arcminutes, with an orientation angle of 110 degrees. Angular size describes how large an object appears on the sky, rather than giving its physical dimensions. The figure can help compare catalogue descriptions, but it is not a guarantee that the whole extent will be visible through any particular instrument. The entry’s size measurement is catalogued with a quality flag of D, which SIMBAD defines as a lower-precision category than its A, B and C flags.

Another important figure in the entry is the redshift: 0.01681333, with a listed uncertainty of 0.0005. Redshift measures the shift of light toward longer wavelengths. It is one of the quantities astronomers use when describing and studying distant objects; it is not something a visual observer can read directly from the galaxy’s appearance. SIMBAD also reports a radial velocity of 4,998 kilometers per second, with an uncertainty of 150 kilometers per second. These values appear together in the database’s optical measurement record.

Taken together, the catalogue details offer several different ways to describe NGC 1275: a name, a position, a morphological label, an active-galaxy classification, an apparent angular extent and a measured redshift. None is a complete account on its own. The coordinates tell where to point a chart; the angular size describes its apparent extent; and the classifications and redshift place it in an astronomical record. Perseus A’s story begins with these carefully distinct pieces of information—and with the reminder that a database entry is a map of what is recorded, not the whole object.
